column3: what it does (an empty field describes the asset type)
column4: status: unknown = the game reads it but what it changes is not known; noeffect = the game never reads it; derived = the editor recomputes it when you save

column3: Plays a sequence: one PlaybackTrack per track, evaluated every update; their poses are merged into one (channel masks OR-ed, later tracks written over earlier ones).
The actor's start settings: a SequenceContainer creates the actor's controller with them, and a container that plays one actor uses them when the caller gave no start settings.
When set, each track's PlaybackTrack and its elements get the actor controller as their parent context.
Sequence length in ticks: the controller's time is clamped to it.
How many tracks the actor has. The game sets up one track per count, so it must match the length of Tracks; the editor keeps the two in step when you save.
The tracks (SequenceAnimTrack); each becomes a PlaybackTrack.

The actor's recorded root path: positions and facing sampled at regular ticks through the sequence. 4,563 of the game's 19,244 actor controllers carry one. What the game uses the path for is not known.
An EnumerationValueAsset: the value of the container's TrackSelectionGameStateEnum for which this actor is the one played.
Bit 9 starts the controller mirrored (XOR with the start settings' mirror flag); bits 10 and 11 select how the tracks are combined while mirrored.
Copied into the ActorController: the first update adds a snap to the start location, then clears it.
Default -1. When >= 0, time past Length calls the controller's loop handler instead of stopping.
One track of a sequence: the target, its warpers and its entries.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
Number of SequenceWarper entries.
The track's SequenceWarpers. A warper with a non-zero TranslateX or TranslateZ turns on trajectory warping for the track.
Number of entries.
The entries in play order. The track's current entry is the last one whose StartTime + EndInTime is at or before the time, and the track ends at the last entry's StartTime + EndInTime.

One entry of a track. It is active on the sequence timeline from StartTime + StartInTime to StartTime + EndInTime; its controller runs at (sequence time - StartTime) x Scale. An entry that starts before the previous one ends is blended in.
The controller played.
The blend used when this entry takes over from the previous one.
Start settings passed to the controller when the entry starts, e.g. a ClipInitParam start tick.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
Sequence time of the entry's in-time 0.
In-time where the entry becomes active; its controller starts at StartInTime x Scale.
In-time where the entry ends.
Controller ticks per sequence tick for this entry.

A sequence: one ActorControllerAsset per actor. What the game creates from it: with TrackSelectionGameStateEnum, only the actor whose TrackSelectionEnumValue matches the enum's current value (the first actor if none does); without it, a SequenceContainer that plays every actor when the container has at least one tag, otherwise only the first actor's controller; a NullController when there are no actors. The SequenceContainer lasts as long as its longest actor and, given a ClipInitParam with a StartTick, is advanced by that many ticks when it is created.
The actors' controllers. Each one is started with its actor's DefaultInitParam.
A GameStateEnumerationAsset. When set, its current value picks the one actor that is played: the first actor whose TrackSelectionEnumValue has that value, else the first actor.
Plays one clip. NumTicks = ceil(clip TrimmedDuration / TimeScale); each update samples the clip at ticks x TimeScale (+ the clip's TrimOffset).
The clip.
Shown by the debugger as TickOffset.
The controller's time is in ticks; TimeScale maps ticks to clip frames.
Clip frames per controller tick: sample frame = ticks x TimeScale + TrimOffset.

How far the clip travels. Speed-scaling controllers divide it by the child's duration and multiply by 60 to get the clip's speed, then time-scale the child so it moves at a requested speed; a BlendArray reports the weight-summed distance of its children.

Bits: 0 = sample with the previous time too (root motion delta), 1 = flag passed to that delta sampling, 3 = looping, 4 = reversed, 5 = passed to the clip setup. The debugger prints bit 3 as Looping and bit 4 as Reversed.
Added to every sample time: frame = controller time x TimeScale + TrimOffset (negative = the first frame is held first).
The playable length in frames: a ClipController lasts ceil(TrimmedDuration / TimeScale) ticks (frames past EndFrame hold the last one).
The clip's codec as four characters: "VBR ", "DCT ", "RAW " or "FRAM".
The ChannelToDofAsset whose DofIds give the rig DOF of each channel of the clip, in channel order (rotations, then vectors, then floats).
The pose layout (DofSetList) the clip's DOFs belong to.
Marks an additive clip (all 12,844 VBR clips are false).
The ClipController's start time in ticks.
Blend duration in ticks.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
Blends from the current pose to the new one over BlendTime ticks; the outgoing pose's weight is curve(CurveType, elapsed / BlendTime).
0 = cos(x*pi/2), 1 = S-curve (21-sample table), 2 = 1 - sin(x*pi/2), 3 = 1 - x (outgoing weight at phase x).
When set, the incoming controller's time is advanced at a phase-matched rate during the blend.
Base of every controller asset; its one field is the controller's tags.
The controller's tags: a TagCollectionSetAsset, resolved.
The tag collections of one or more controllers.
The tag collections.
Base of the tag collections (Default, BranchOut, BranchIn).
The collection's tags; 2,884 BranchIn collections hold BranchInPointTags, 16,029 BranchOut collections BranchOutPointTags, 18,354 Default collections the rest.
The tags in this collection. The game checks every one of them on each update while the clip plays, so each tag's window opens and closes on time.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
The tag collection a controller uses by default: the tags it monitors every update, plus the flag that says some of them are exit tags.
Resolved as a bool game-state value.

A tag the game watches while its clip plays. On every update it checks whether the playhead is inside the tag's window, and acts when the window opens, while it is open, and when it closes - passing along how far through the window it is, from 0 at the start to 1 at the end.
Base of every tag with a time.

Where the tag's window starts, in the owner controller's ticks (a sequence's ticks on an ActorControllerAsset, the controller's ticks on a ClipControllerAsset). Read as 0 when LinkFlags has 0x80; a fraction of the owner's length when LinkFlags has 0x40.

0x80: the window starts at 0 (StartLinkOffset ignored). 0x40: start and length are fractions of the owner's length. Values in the game's data: 0x20 x91,207, 0xA0 x7,496, 0 x3,072, 0x10 x655, 0x80 x438, 0x40 x40, 0x90 x1.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
A TimelinePointTag with a length.

The window's length, not its end time: the branch code computes start + phase x EndLinkOffset, and 52,093 of 96,152 sequence tags have EndLinkOffset < StartLinkOffset. Scaled like the start when LinkFlags has 0x40.

A state machine. One node plays at a time; on each update the current node's animation advances and its transitions are tried. When a transition fires partway through an update, the rest of that update's time goes to the new node, so switches happen on the exact frame.
The node the machine starts in. A node that is no machine's StartNode gets empty flattened tables.

The machine's own id, and the value a BranchTypeAsset's ControllerFilterIdentifier is matched against: a branch window whose type filters on a different identifier cannot fire a transition of this machine. It is derived from the asset's key - xor (key >> 32) - which reproduces all 96 the game's controllers, so the editor recomputes it on save.
True when any of the machine's nodes has NodeType 3, which reproduces all 96 the game's controllers, so the editor recomputes it on save. 44 of the game's 96 machines use gate nodes.
Every one of the game's 96 controllers has 5.
A bool game state or signal: 6 of the game's 96 controllers name one.
An operation. Empty in every controller.

The machine's default blend. It is the last fallback of the blend choice: a transition's OverrideBlend, or the branch type's blend, is used first. 88 of the game's 96 controllers share one blend asset, 8 have none.
A GameStateEnumerationAsset, which goes with EnumToGUIDMap and the nodes' EnumValue. Empty in every controller, so the whole enum path is unused in the game's data.
A bool game state. Empty in every controller.
Nodes indexed by the enum's value. Empty in every controller.
A debug flag; false in every controller.
A flag; false in every controller.

The node's transitions as the game tries them: a tree (FirstChildIndex, SiblingIndex) walked from entry 0; of the entries that can fire, the one that fires earliest in the update wins, the earlier one on a tie.
Every condition this node's transitions test. Each one is checked at most once per update and the answer reused, so many transitions can share a condition cheaply.
The branch types this node's transitions wait for. The first three entries are placeholders; the rest are the real types. The editor recomputes this list when you save.

One state of a state machine: what it plays (SubjectController), the transitions out of it and the conditions they test. NodeType says whether it is a normal state, a conduit (a junction with no animation of its own) or a gate.
The state machine the node belongs to.
What the node plays while it is the current state. Its length and its branch windows are what end-of-clip and branch-window transitions are timed against.
The start settings handed to the subject.

The transitions out of this node. The game does not walk this list directly - it uses FlattenedTransitions, which the editor builds from it when you save. For a conduit, these transitions are folded into every node that leads to it.
Authoring data for the original tool: one entry per transition.
An operation the node runs. 3 of the game's 1,622 nodes set it.
Conditions that must all be true for the machine to enter this node. They are checked together with the conditions of the transition leading here, before that transition fires.
Conditions that must all be false for the machine to enter this node.
Signals this node turns on while it is the current state. When exactly they are turned off again is not known.

0 a state, 1 a conduit (it has no subject of its own; the nodes that transition to it take its transitions as the children of that entry), 3 a gate (an entry that goes through it also needs the gate's own check). A state machine with any NodeType 3 node has UsesGateNodes set.
0 in every node in the game's data. What it changes is not known.
Conditions (indices into AllTransitionConditions) that must all be true for the entry; they include the target node's entry conditions.
Conditions that must all be false for the entry.

When the entry can fire in the update: 0 at once; 1 (BranchAtEnd) at the playing animation's time left minus the transition's BranchAtEndOffset; 2 (BranchAfterFirstUpdate) at once except in the node's first update; 3 and up inside a window of a BranchOutPointTag on the playing animation's timeline whose BranchTypeAsset is AllBranchTypes[index].

Which entry starts this entry's children (a conduit's transitions, or a nested machine's start). A parent fires only once its chosen child can fire too. An entry with no children points past the end of the table. The editor recomputes this when you save.
The next entry at the same level of the tree; pointing past the end of the table ends the level. The editor recomputes this when you save.
255 means no gate. Otherwise the transition also has to pass its gate node's check; what that check tests is not known. The editor recomputes this when you save.

One entry of a node's transition table - the form the game actually uses. The editor builds this table from the node's Transitions, the transitions' From/To and the conditions when you save, so you never need to edit it by hand.

The node the entry leads to - the transition's To, or, for the nested entry a node with a state-machine subject gets, that machine's StartNode. Resolved as StateFlowNodeControllerAsset. For a gate entry it is also the gate node whose check must pass.
The transition this entry stands for; 0 for a nested entry. The fire time reads BranchAtEndOffset from it.
Empty in every entry in the game's data. What a gate does with it is not known.
Set on the one entry a node with a state-machine subject gets for that machine's StartNode. The editor's run skips these, so nested machines are not followed there.
Ticks before the end of the node's controller at which a BranchAtEnd transition fires.

One transition of a state machine: from which node, to which, under what conditions and when it may fire. The game uses these through the node's transition table, which the editor rebuilds from them when you save.
The node the transition leaves. It decides which node's transition table the transition is placed in.
The node the transition goes to. It is also the TransitionNode of the derived FlattenedTransitions entry.
Conditions that must all be true for the transition to fire.
Conditions that must all be false for the transition to fire.

The branch type whose window the transition waits for. Set, it makes the flattened entry's BranchTypeIndex point at this type in the node's AllBranchTypes, and the transition can only fire while a BranchOutPointTag of the subject with that BranchTypeAsset is open (and only if the type's ControllerFilterIdentifier is 0 or the state machine's Identifier).
A second branch type for the destination side. Only 3 of the game's 3,737 transitions set it, and what it changes is not known.

Fire when the leaving node's subject reaches its end. It becomes BranchTypeIndex 1 in the flattened entry (when BranchWindowTypeAsset is empty), and the fire time is the playing animation's time left minus BranchAtEndOffset.

Fire at any time except during the node's first update. It becomes BranchTypeIndex 2 (when BranchWindowTypeAsset and BranchAtEnd are not set), where the fire time is 0, or 1e35 (never) while the node's first-update flag is set.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.

The blend used when this transition fires. It is picked by walking the chosen flattened entry and its parents: the first transition along that chain with an OverrideBlend set wins; failing that the branch type's own blend is asked for; failing that the state machine's BlendTag is used.
A TagCollectionSetAsset, so the transition can bring tag collections of its own.
A float: how far into the new node's subject to start.
A FloatAsset, a destination phase read from the game instead of the fixed one.
What it changes is not known.
Which state machine may use windows of this type: 0 means any, otherwise the transition only fires when the machine's Identifier matches.

A branch type: the name a BranchOutPointTag window and a transition's BranchWindowTypeAsset agree on, plus the tuning either side of the window and the state machine it is restricted to. 48 in the game's data.
The tuner that shifts the window's ends. The editor's state-machine run does not model it and uses the untuned window.
A second tuner, the same type as BranchTuner.
A branch window on a controller's timeline: a state machine transition with the same branch type can fire while the controller's time is inside it.
The branch type of the window: transitions whose BranchWindowTypeAsset is this type use it.

The state machine's own branch windows ignore this. Other parts of the game that look for branch-out points (dribbling, previews, warps) only take tags with Active set. False on every tag in the game's data.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
The start settings the ActorPreviewController creates TargetAsset with; also read by the DribbleController ctor.
The controller that follows an Active branch tag in the ActorPreviewController.

When above 0, gameplay code picks the branch time inside [window start, start + StartTuningOffset] from a 0..1 value of the player object: time = min(start + StartTuningOffset, start + 30 x (1 - value)).
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.
The game reads this, but what it changes is not known.

Plays one of its entries, picked by its policy (random, by an enumeration, or by signals). With none of ChooseOnReset, ChooseEveryUpdate, ChooseFirstUpdate and Looping set, it picks once when it starts - the last entry if the policy picks none - and never changes.
The policy that picks the entry.
The entries, in the order the policies scan them.
Receives the chosen index.

When set, the chooser can pick again on every update. Exactly how it re-picks is not known.

The controller the entry plays.

Random pick by weight: r = a 16-bit random number from the game state of RandomValueAsset / 65535 x the sum of the weights; the entries' weights are subtracted in order and the first that brings r to 0 or below is chosen. No positive weight: none.
The game state the random number is read from.
The entry's share of the random pick.
One entry of a random chooser: the animation to play and its weight. A higher weight makes the entry more likely to be picked.
Picks the first entry whose enumeration value equals the value of GameStateAsset (an integer game state); an entry without a value is the default; game state -1: none.
The integer game state compared with the entries' values.
The value this entry is for (the value object's Value); none: this is the default entry.
One entry of an EnumChooserPolicyAsset: the enumeration value that selects it. 70 in the game's data; an entry with no value is the policy's default.
Picks the first entry whose TrueSignals are all on and FalseSignals all off; none: none.
Keeps the previous entry while its signals still hold (if it has any).
Signals that must all be on for this entry.
Signals that must all be off for this entry.

Runs its layers' controllers and combines their poses in layer order.
Each layer's controller.
Each layer's weight (a float signal); a layer whose weight is 1.5e-5 or less is not updated unless its UpdateMode is 1.
Each layer's blend mask - which joints the layer affects. How the mask is applied is not known.

When each layer runs. 0: never. 1: always, even at weight 0. 2: only while its weight is above 0. 3: as 2, and at weight 0 the layer is told so (what that does is not known). In the game's data, 220 layers use 2 and 26 use 1.

How the layer's time advances (phase = time / length): 0 by the update's time; 1 to the first layer's phase; 2 to the previous layer's phase; 3 by the first layer's phase change; 4 by the previous layer's phase change. In the game's data,: 0 x210, 1 x36.

A celebration candidate of a UCC state: when asked whether it is available it runs Expression, reads MinCDBScore, checks UCCUnlockableComponent (unavailable when that check fails) and runs PostExpression; when chosen it makes ControllerAsset's controller and passes it to AnimLaunchedCallback.
The controller (a celebration sequence) this candidate plays: point it at another SequenceContainerAsset to play another celebration here.
An expression run first when the candidate is checked.
An expression run after the checks pass.
Its check must pass for the candidate to be available (the celebration's unlock).

Told about the controller made for the candidate.
A gate node's chooser: asks DistillPolicy for what to play and post-processes the result.
The policy that answers the gate.
Which feet to reset. 0 (used by 4,591 of the game's 4,683 tags) means both feet, 1 and 2 mean one foot each. Any other value means none - 48 and 64 occur in the game's data and do nothing.
A tag that resets the foot planting. 4,683 in the game's data.
Plays an animation in a loop, restarting it each time it reaches its end (or LoopEndTime).
The looped child. The LoopingController creates it with its own start settings and copies the child's time and duration into its own.
The looping controller ignores this and passes its own start settings to the animation it loops.
When set, LoopEndTime (if it is not past the child's duration) replaces the child's end as the loop point, and after each restart the child is advanced by LoopStartTime.
On the first update the child is advanced by StartTime ticks before the frame's own update.
Ticks the child is advanced right after it restarts (only with IsLoopControl and when above 0).

The loop point, in the looped animation's ticks (only with IsLoopControl). When the playhead crosses it, the animation is restarted and jumps to LoopStartTime, and the rest of that update plays on from there. The two poses may be blended across the jump.
Mirrors an animation left to right, and flips the values listed in its MirrorListAsset while doing so. With a PhaseOffset between 0 and 1 the mirrored copy also runs that far ahead.
The animation that is mirrored. It gets the same start settings as the mirror controller.

An AssetListAsset of game-state values. While the child is created and on every update, each element's value is written into an override context negated: a bool as its opposite, a float with its sign bit flipped, an integer as its negative.

Below 1.5258789e-05 or above 0.99998474 a plain MirrorController is made; otherwise a MirrorPhaseOffsetController keeps the child offset by this fraction of its duration (its time is derived from PhaseOffset and the child's phase and duration).
Plays an animation locked to a phase: it moves the animation to whatever time its sync points give for the current phase. With NumCycles of 2 or more it covers several cycles.
The animation that is played. It gets the same start settings as this controller, with SubjectControllerInit added.
Extra start settings handed to the played animation.

The sync points as fractions of the played animation's length (0 = start, 1 = end). Each update the controller finds the two points around the current phase and sets the animation's time between them.
When set, the output pose is mirrored.
How many cycles the sync points cover: fewer than 2 gives a SyncPointController, otherwise a MultiCycleSyncPointController; sync points per cycle = (count - 1) / NumCycles + 1.
Outputs a still default pose - what other controllers fall back on when they have nothing to play. Its time runs from 0 to 1 and stops there.
The layout whose default pose is output.
Plays a child controller started at a phase offset.
The animation that is played. It gets the same start settings as this controller.
Where the child starts, as a fraction of its duration: the ctor keeps the fractional part of the wrapped value and the reset sets the child's time to it x the child's duration.
One move of a street move group: plays its animation on a phase that its speed, start phase and phase count turn into a time in the animation.
The animation that is played.
Playback rate of the child: the item's time is the child's time / ItemSpeed and its duration the child's duration / ItemSpeed / NumPhase, so each item tick moves the child ItemSpeed ticks.
Phase offset, in units of one of the child's NumPhase cycles, added before the phase is mapped to the child's time.
Adds half a cycle to the phase and mirrors the output pose.
How many cycles the child holds: the item's cycle is the child's duration / NumPhase and its phase wraps at NumPhase.

The delta column, resolved the same way; the operation built from it carries IKControllerOffset instead of the weights. In all 10,119 the game's tags that set it, DeltaIndex is ReachIndex - 1.

The ramp before the tag's window, in the tag's own time unit. The pass takes d = (current time) - (the tag's start); when d is positive it subtracts the tag's length and clamps at 0, so d is 0 inside the window, negative before it and positive after it. For d < 0 the IK weight is 1 - (-d / IKBlendIn) while -d <= IKBlendIn, and 0 further out. Values in the game's data: run 0 to 20.

The ramp after the window: for d >= 0 the IK weight is 1 - (d / IKBlendOut) while d <= IKBlendOut, and 0 beyond. The test needs IKBlendOut greater than 0 before any weight is set, so a tag with IKBlendOut 0 applies no IK at all, not even inside its own window. 17 of the game's 8,194 TouchTags have 0, so those apply no IK at all; the rest run 1 to 22.
